title: Also wasn’t including non-English versions 😬 #shakespeare #hamlet #fi...
transcript: Ranking film adaptations of Hamlet from worst to best, but first, three honorable mentions: I'm not including pro-shots in this ranking, but for the record, the Andrew Scott / Robert Icke version is my favorite Hamlet in any form, full stop. I'm also not including made for TV Versions, but the David Tennant one is pretty solid. And I'm not including loose reimaginings. But of course you gotta love The Lion King. Easily in last place the 1990 Mel Gibson version. And I'm sorry, I think this movie sucks. His performance is atrocious and the screenplay adaptation is a disjointed mess. In fifth place the 1969 Tony Richardson film. Which, to be clear, is a lot better than the Mel Gibson one. In fact, I was tempted to rank this one even higher because it's well acted, it moves at a good pace, and the tight, almost claustrophobic camera work definitely has a distinct effect, but otherwise there's not a whole lot setting it apart as a film. As far as I can tell, it was not a made for TV Movie, but it kinda has the vibe of one. In fourth place the Ethan Hawke one directed by Michael Almereyda. It's very vibey. It evokes a strong sense of place and time and mood, but sometimes in a way that can feel a little too thin and hollow. In third place the one that just came out starring Riz Ahmed, directed by Aneil Karia. Similar to the Ethan Hawke one, It uses a modern setting, it's very brooding, it's heavily abridged, maybe to a fault, but it has more interesting ideas than the Ethan Hawke one, just generally more to say. In second place, Lawrence Olivier’s 1948 film, which is not one that I connect to very strongly personally. It feels a little dated, it drags in some places, but it's a solid, pretty straightforward film adaptation of the play, with some amusing stylistic choices sprinkled in to spice things up. And I think Olivier’s performance as Hamlet is probably the best on this list. It's mercurial and unsettling, but also very charismatic. Ok before you judge my number one pick, I have to explain my reasoning. It kinda kills me to put Kenneth Branagh's 1996 film in first place because I have beef with him. I think his performance as Hamlet is like Razzie-level bad, maybe even worse than Mel Gibson. But if I'm thinking in terms of which of these films strikes the best balance between faithfully honoring the text and optimizing the medium of cinema, I gotta go with this one. And to be clear, the mere fact that he included every word from Hamlet is not what I mean by “faithful,” because I'm all for cutting down Shakespeare. It's that as a director he really commits to it in a thoughtful way. He doesn't treat anything like filler. And while it's not the most sophisticated take on Hamlet, I do think it's successful as a piece of Hollywood popcorn entertainment, it's probably the Hamlet film that I'd be most inclined to just press “play” on at any given moment. Although I would also be pressing “fast forward” through his soliloquies, which is admittedly a shame.
